claim: Resource-rational analysis picks the procedure maximising expected result minus the expected cost of computing; the optimisation is done by evolution/learning, not on the spot, so it is a design target, not a runnable per-problem rule.
agent_test: Compare an S0 gate using a cheap learned difficulty predictor against always-deliberate and never-deliberate at equal total tokens.
audit_note: Minor: 'design target, not a runnable per-problem rule' is interpretation: Lieder and Griffiths say Eq. 3 is a problem solved by evolution and learning rather than by the person, while Gershman et al. (not re-opened, blocked) describe online metalevel stopping; a01, a02, a03 and b01 are the same paper, so independent sources are Lieder and Griffiths plus Russell and Subramanian.

claim: People choose between strategies in a cost-sensitive way: they pick merge sort when it is faster (83% of N=100, 95% CI 74.9-89.4) and pick heuristics by learned expected quality minus cost (64.6% correct, N=120).
agent_test: Give the agent a menu of procedures with token costs; test whether a learned selector beats a fixed procedure at equal tokens. Evidence is one lab (Lieder/Griffiths); no independent replication found. Gap search 2019-2026: no independent replication of the cost-sensitivity result found; nearest is Xie and Moss 2025 (N=144) replicating success-rate-driven strategy choice in a different theory.

claim: The best number of mental samples per decision is very small: Vul et al. (2014) show one sample is optimal when execution takes less than about 10 times as long as sampling under a symmetric utility (Lieder and Griffiths' review reports a threshold of about 3x), and the effective number of samples rises with stakes (r(25)=.61 across probability-matching studies).
agent_test: Vary the stakes and sample cost in prompts; check whether sample count (self-consistency k) should scale with stakes. Optimal k=1 holds for symmetric utility and ratio under 10 (Vul et al.).
audit_note: The 3x threshold appears only in Lieder and Griffiths' review (a04 and b03 are the same text); the primary paper (Vul et al. 2014) says one sample is optimal for action/sample time ratios below 10 under a symmetric utility, and that no sampling pays off below a ratio of 2 with no penalty for errors, so the threshold depends on the utility function.
claim_before_audit: The best number of mental samples per decision is very small; one sample is bounded-optimal when acting takes at most about 3x as long as sampling, and more samples pay off with higher stakes.

claim: Anchoring can be fit as an optimal speed-accuracy stop in sequential adjustment (ten phenomena); fitted adjustment counts differ widely between datasets (8 vs 29), so the explanation is flexible.
agent_test: Not directly testable on the agent; use as a caution that cost-parameters are fitted post hoc.

claim: People plan close to a cost-sensitive optimal model, with systematic departures: in Callaway et al. Exp 1 (95 analysed) they earned 0.92 points below the Pareto front at the same click count, expanded a maximal-value path 81.5% of the time, and 45 were best fit by the optimal model vs 41 by best-first. The earlier '86% of best trade-off, 55% strategy agreement' figures were not found in the primary paper.
agent_test: Do not cite 86% or 55%. Use best-first expansion with a cost-based stop as the planning default and measure our own gap to a cost-aware oracle.

claim: Learned metalevel policies (BMPS) reach 98-99% of optimal return in small simulated worlds, beating meta-greedy by 6.8-35.8% and full deliberation (0.20 vs 0.65), and pay for their own overhead when object-level computation is much costlier.
agent_test: Only the original authors; domains are tiny. Test a VOC-style stopping policy on agent tool calls at equal tokens.

claim: Training an LLM with a value-of-computation reward (log-prob gain minus 0.1 per token) cuts tokens 23-32% vs STaR (35-42% vs few-shot CoT) at equal or slightly better accuracy (8B: 63.5% vs 61.9%; 3B 50.1% vs 47.4%).
agent_test: One paper (re-verified directly); training-based, so not applicable to a scaffold-only agent. Out-of-distribution accuracy mixed (8B on MMLU-CF 36.4 vs 40.2).

claim: Reasoning length should adapt to difficulty: RaM spends 36-50% fewer tokens on easy items, STaR 34-36%, few-shot CoT 19-24%, instruction-tuned CoT prompting about 0.5-0.9% (no adaptation).
agent_test: Measure token ratio hard/easy for the agent with and without an S0 gate; the target is a large ratio with no accuracy loss.

claim: Reasoning models overthink easy questions: 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on 2+3, first solution already correct in over 92% of cases; self-training removes 35-48% of tokens at near-equal accuracy.
agent_test: Log the stage at which the first correct answer appears; test early-stop at the first verified answer.
audit_note: All numbers verified (1,953%, over 92%, 48.6% MATH500 and 35-46% on GSM8K/GPQA/AIME with small accuracy changes), but b15, b16, c09 and c10 are the same paper (Chen et al. 2412.21187); the survey and Cuadron et al. (agentic overthinking) do not report these figures, so the claim rests on one paper.

claim: Dynamic early exit and confidence probes shorten reasoning with no accuracy loss: DEER 19-43% fewer tokens (+0.3 to +5.0 accuracy); hidden-state probe 24% fewer tokens at 88.2%; shortest of k chains up to 34.5% more accurate than longest.
agent_test: Compare a stop-when-confident rule against fixed budget at equal tokens; the shortest-chain-wins rule is a cheap selector.
audit_note: Minor: DEER's 19.1-42.9% shorter paired with +0.9 to +4.8 accuracy for the three main models; +0.3 to +5.0 is the all-model range, and 'no accuracy loss' holds on average for these methods rather than every setting. b24 and d05 are the same probing paper.

claim: Sequential stopping of self-consistency saves samples without accuracy loss: Adaptive-Consistency about 3.3x fewer samples (0.07 point drop, 17 datasets); window early-stopping 34-84% fewer samples.
agent_test: Replace fixed k with a stop-when-leading-answer-stable rule and compare at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: c17 and d10 are the same Adaptive-Consistency paper, so independent sources are Adaptive-Consistency and ESC; figures match (3.3x avg, 3.2x in Table 5, 0.07 mean accuracy drop, ESC 33.8-84.2%).

claim: Allocating test-time compute by prompt difficulty beats uniform best-of-N with about 4x less compute, and a small model with extra compute can beat a 14x larger one on easy and medium items.
agent_test: Estimate difficulty from a cheap first pass and route budget; compare to uniform best-of-N at equal tokens. Gains concentrate in easy/medium items.
audit_note: Both snell entries (b19, c07) are the same paper (Snell et al. 2408.03314) and the sleep-time paper does not support the claim; figures match the abstract (more than 4x efficiency vs best-of-N, outperforms a 14x larger model in a FLOPs-matched test where the small model has non-trivial success).

claim: More thinking is not monotonic: gains then losses (R1-Distill-1.5B GSM8K 82.2 -> 87.3 -> 70.3%), inverse scaling in some tasks, and parallel voting beats longer chains at the same budget.
agent_test: Cap reasoning length and compare a long chain to parallel short chains at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: the 82.2 to 87.3 to 70.3 curve and the parallel-voting advantage (up to 20-22%) come from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B on GSM8K/MATH-500; Gema et al. confirm inverse scaling on specific task families only (the claim says 'some tasks').

claim: Explicit budget prompts can cut length about 68% (TALE) but too small a budget backfires (token elasticity); length-controlled RL (L1) gives smooth accuracy-vs-budget, and a max-budget wastes fewer tokens than an exact one. Prompt-only budgets help only inside a band: DEER reports token-budget prompts fail on AIME24 (models write longer than vanilla), while a budget display (Budget Tracker) works for agents (BrowseComp 12.8% at 10 calls vs 12.6% at 100 for ReAct, 31.3% lower cost).
agent_test: Test a prompt-level budget estimate versus no budget; sweep the budget to find the elasticity point.
audit_note: Minor: 'Prompt-only budgets help only inside a band' is the author's synthesis of TALE token elasticity and the DEER AIME24 remark; the TALE -68% is for GPT-4o-mini averaged over datasets, with accuracy 83.75 to 81.03; Budget Tracker result is Gemini-2.5-Pro on BrowseComp.

claim: Frontier LLMs fail to allocate a shared budget across problems: oracle allocation beat actual contest play in 71 of 72 cells (R3-Bench), and reasoning models persist on hard items where humans disengage. Fan et al. 2026 (7 models, Omni-MATH exam) find the same: effort follows presentation order (rho -0.34 to -0.48 with position, 0.00 to +0.11 with point value) and a planning prompt does not add value-awareness. A 1.5B model trained for solve-or-skip (ROI-Reasoning) closes much of the gap, so the failure is fixable but not by prompting alone.
agent_test: Build the allocator in the scaffold (rank by estimated value per cost, per-item cap, explicit skip) and test against a prompt-only planner on a 10-20 item shared budget.
audit_note: Minor: Fan et al.'s position correlation is -0.34 overall and -0.17/-0.38/-0.48 for N=5/10/20, so the quoted -0.34 to -0.48 mixes overall and N=20 values; the ROI-Reasoning test is a different 3-problem setup than Fan's, so 'fixable' is an inference across studies.

claim: Fine-grained strategy choice in LLMs is not purely human-like: models over-assume human rationality (corr 0.94 with expected value vs 0.48 for people) and a plain LLM misses human bandit regret unless fine-tuned.
agent_test: Caution for any use of an LLM as a model of human resource-rational behaviour; not a test of the agent.
audit_note: Minor: 0.94 is GPT-4o with chain-of-thought (other settings lower, e.g. zero-shot 0.28), on risky-choice problems, not bandits; sources b25/c22 are the same paper.

claim: Critics in the BBS commentaries note that resource-rational models add degrees of freedom (resource costs), and Lieder and Griffiths acknowledge that falsification is hard in practice and the approach is hard to apply where constraints or the environment are unknown; no count of independent replications was found in the sources read.
agent_test: Pre-register cost parameters before testing any gate, to avoid post hoc fitting.
audit_note: Critic points are supported (commentators warn of added degrees of freedom in specifying resource costs; Lieder and Griffiths concede falsification is hard when constraints are uncertain and RRA is hard to apply when environment or constraints are unknown), but 'no count of independent replications exists' is an absence claim that none of the sources establish; the Vul et al. entry is unrelated.
claim_before_audit: Critics note resource-rational models add free cost parameters, are hard to falsify, and the approach is hard to apply where constraints or environment are unknown; no count of independent replications exists.

claim: Monitor-style or sleep-time compute can move or avoid live cost: sleep-time compute gives same accuracy with about 5x less test-time compute (up to +13%/+18% when scaled), while Oh and Gobet's monitor-generate-verify is a proposal with no data. Pay-back needs many related, predictable queries per context: cost per query falls up to 2.5x at 10 queries per context and the gain shrinks with few queries or unpredictable ones.
agent_test: Precompute reusable context summaries offline and compare token use per query.

claim: Zero-cost confidence gates are domain-bound: a hidden-state probe cuts about 24% of tokens at 88.2% accuracy (threshold 0.85) but does not stably transfer from logic to math, and the 16-trace warm-up of DeepConf is a fixed gate cost that only pays against a large reference N (512).
agent_test: Measure first-pass-confidence or trial-answer gating on a mixed task set at equal total tokens, counting the gate's own tokens.

claim: Early-exit and 'think less' gains do not automatically carry to agentic work: on SWE-bench Verified, o1 at low effort had 35% higher overthinking than at high effort, yet choosing the lower-overthinking of 2 low-effort runs gave 27.3% at $800 vs 29.1% at $1,400 for high effort.
agent_test: For agent steps, cap private reasoning and prefer an action that returns feedback; compare against a no-cap run on 20+ tasks.

claim: Stopping-rule cost differs: the Beta rule in Adaptive-Consistency takes about 0.03 ms per decision (as does the entropy rule; the Dirichlet and CRP rules take about 95-101 ms), while DEER's trial-answer probing adds overhead that its branch-parallel variant reduces (latency cut 27.9-40.1% for original DEER vs 36.3-58.6% for branch-parallel, on MATH-500 and AMC), so probe overhead should be counted.
agent_test: Count probe tokens inside the budget; prefer vote-count rules when several samples already exist.
audit_note: Beta 0.03 ms is real (but Entropy rule is also 0.03 ms; Dirichlet/CRP ~95-101 ms). DEER latency cut 27.9-40.1% was measured on MATH-500/AMC, while the 19.1-42.9% token cut spans all benchmarks; the ranges overlap, and the paper says latency speedup vs length savings is superlinear, so 'latency only' is not supported.
claim_before_audit: Stopping-rule cost: the Beta rule in Adaptive-Consistency takes 0.03 ms (negligible), while trial-answer probes (DEER) cut tokens 19-43% but latency only 27.9-40.1%, so probe overhead is real and must be counted.

claim: No source compares Adaptive-Consistency, DEER and a value-of-computation threshold at equal tokens; the ranking for our scaffold is unknown.
agent_test: Run the three rules at one fixed token budget on a mixed task set; this is the open experiment.

claim: Budget-aware prompting without training is feasible for agents (Budget Tracker: +18.6 points on SWE at budget 50, 55.4% vs 36.8%, similar calls), whereas a bare token cap can backfire (token elasticity; TALE estimate in range only 60.61% of the time).
agent_test: Show remaining budget at each step; sweep token-cap size to find the turn where tokens rise.

claim: Offline precomputation pays only for shared, predictable contexts: sleep-time compute lowers cost per query up to 2.5x at 10 queries per context, with a gap that grows with predictability.
agent_test: Cache problem restatement/decomposition only when 3+ later steps reuse it.

claim: Cost parameters can be set from outside the model: Lieder et al. 2018 varied time cost and error cost independently and adjustment moved in the predicted directions, though no independent replication exists and the sample sizes were not read.
agent_test: Pre-register explicit time and error prices for the gate and test the predicted direction, no post hoc fitting.
